contests.title: Member Of City Council #2, Fremont

candidates.name: Desrie Campbell
candidates.who: Incumbent councilmember and former school board member; 30-year Fremont resident. Promises to expand parks and open space, fix roads and pedestrian infrastructure, support local businesses and manufacturing, and keep climate commitments. Lists endorsements from Rep. Ro Khanna and Assemblymember Alex Lee.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Keith Parker
candidates.who: Marketing director and 30-year resident; PTSA board member and on the Ohlone College, Washington Health and Fremont Education foundation boards. Names homelessness, departing businesses and crime as the top problems; proposes individualized homelessness services, more police staffing and faster permitting for businesses.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

contests.title: Member Of City Council #3, Fremont

candidates.name: Kathy Kimberlin
candidates.who: Appointed to the Council in 2024; Fremont field director for the Alameda County Supervisor. Focuses on traffic, services for unhoused residents, small businesses, nonprofit partnerships and public safety. Lists endorsements from Rep. Ro Khanna, Treasurer Fiona Ma, Assemblymember Alex Lee and the Tri-City mayors.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Vipin Sharma
candidates.who: Senior engineering manager (in engineering since 1991) with physics degrees; volunteers with Fremont Police's VIPS program. Pitches an independent, evidence-based approach to public safety, homelessness and budgeting, and promises to explain the reasoning behind decisions.

candidates.name: Aziz Akbari
candidates.who: Director on the Alameda County Water District board for a decade; grew up in Fremont public schools. Points to $30M+ in infrastructure grants, a low-income rate program and a AAA bond rating there; wants affordable housing for working families and seniors, more green space and fiscal transparency.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Ying Min Li
candidates.who: Small business owner and former Silicon Valley engineer; 30-year resident. Public safety is the top priority (a fully staffed police department), followed by traffic congestion and moving people from homelessness into stable housing.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Manisha Pathak
candidates.who: Tech-industry veteran of 20 years, Fremont Human Relations Commissioner, nonprofit founder and teacher of Indian classical music. Priorities: homelessness with measurable results, first-responder and community partnerships, traffic infrastructure, practical environmental steps.

contests.title: Mayor, Oakland

candidates.name: Brenda F. Grisham
candidates.who: Lifelong Oaklander and owner of a financial-services firm. After a son's 2010 killing, became a public-safety and victims' advocate (Violence Prevention Coalition chair, Ceasefire speaker, East Bay Alliance for Public Safety). Runs on public safety and financial stability.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Barbara Lee
candidates.who: Incumbent mayor (elected 2025), former Congresswoman, state senator and assemblymember. Credits the administration with governance reform (Charter Reform), reduced gun violence, 7,000 tons of trash removed by volunteers and budget stability, and pledges to protect Oakland from federal threats.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Mindy Ruth Pechenuk
candidates.who: Educator and researcher. Proposes reviving manufacturing and trade apprenticeships, a full independent audit, spending cuts without new taxes, and ending camera-ticket revenue ("treating drivers like cash machines"); promises to confront open-air drug markets.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

candidates.name: Julius Robinson
candidates.who: Banking and community-development consultant; near-40-year resident. Cites $200M+ in community development programs and a $350M investment fund; runs on safe neighborhoods, accountable government, business growth and housing.

who_source.label: Candidate's statement in the official county voter guide

Lists endorsements from the mayor and the entire council.

contests.title: Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance.
contests.fiscal: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.
contests.yes_means: The state could borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.
contests.no_means: The state could not borrow $11.25 billion to support veterans and affordable housing.

official_args.for: Prop. 1 builds affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities, low- and middle-income working families, vulnerable Californians and essential workers—teachers, firefighters and nurses. Expands homeownership opportunities, fast-tracks affordable shovel-ready homes, helps those one crisis away from homelessness. Requires strict fiscal accountability and public oversight with no new taxes.
official_args.against: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED.

contests.listed_supporters: US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services

contests.title: Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns.
contests.fiscal: State budget reserves would be higher.
contests.yes_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.
contests.no_means: Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

official_args.for: Vote yes on Proposition 2 to protect schools, healthcare, and public safety funding. Proposition 2 doubles the state's Rainy Day Fund, stops politicians from overspending when there is a budget surplus, and ensures education funding continues during economic downturns. It has bipartisan support from firefighters, hospitals, health clinics, and educators.
official_args.against: Proposition 2 guarantees more spending, not savings, creating a loophole that makes taxpayer rebates less likely by excluding reserve deposits from California's constitutional spending limit. It provides no new funding for education, healthcare, or public safety. Vote No to protect taxpayer rebates and constitutional limits.

contests.listed_supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel

sources.label: CA Official Voter Information Guide — Prop 2

contests.title: Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
contests.summary: Makes permanent existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 (adjusted annually for inflation). Allocates tax revenues to public education.
contests.fiscal: Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.
contests.yes_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
contests.no_means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.

official_args.for: PROPOSITION 3 PROTECTS OUR SCHOOLS AND HEALTHCARE WITHOUT RAISING YOUR TAXES. Prop. 3 prevents a massive tax cut for millionaires and billionaires by maintaining the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% have paid for 15 years and requires strict accountability and audits to ensure school funding gets to classrooms. Vote YES.
official_args.against: Californians already pay the nation’s highest income, sales, and gas taxes—and have the highest cost of living. Prop. 3 makes temporary income taxes permanent while Sacramento wastes billions on failed programs instead of voters’ priorities. Don’t reward failure. Fix spending first before making taxes permanent. No on Prop. 3.

contests.title: Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety.
contests.fiscal: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs.
contests.yes_means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
contests.no_means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.

official_args.for: YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
official_args.against: Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.

contests.title: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
contests.placed_by: Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
contests.summary: Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment.
contests.fiscal: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled.
contests.yes_means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
contests.no_means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

official_args.for: Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
official_args.against: Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

contests.title: Regional Transit Measure
contests.question: To prevent major service cuts to BART and other transit, avoid increased traffic, and reduce pollution by: Preserving BART, Caltrain, VTA, SamTrans, AC Transit, Muni, other transit for everyone, including workers, students, seniors, persons with disabilities; Supporting transit safety, cleanliness, affordability, reliability; Repairing targeted roads/potholes; Requiring financial transparency, oversight, accountability; shall the measure enacting a 0.5% (Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, Santa Clara counties), and 1% (San Francisco) sales tax for 14 years generating approximately $980,000,000 annually, be adopted?
contests.threshold: 50%+1 of all votes cast in the five Bay Area counties
contests.proposal: This measure was placed on the ballot by voter initiative, signed by the requisite number of voters within the Public Transit Revenue Measure District (“District”). The District was created by the Legislature through Senate Bill 63 (“SB 63”) in 2025 (Government Code sections 67700-67788), which was enacted to preserve and improve public transit service in the San Francisco Bay Area. The District comprises the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and is governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission (“MTC”). SB 63 authorizes District voters to approve a retail transactions and use tax (commonly referred to as a sales tax) for specified purposes. This measure would impose a tax of 0.5% in the counties of Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara and 1.0% in the City and County of San Francisco. The tax would be imposed and collected in largely the same manner as a state-imposed sales tax. The tax would be in effect for 14 years and would not count toward the statutory limit on combined local sales tax rates. It is estimated that the tax would raise approximately $980 million per year. After payment of defined costs, including election costs and administrative expenses, the District must transfer all remaining revenues to MTC and county transportation agencies for distribution and expenditure according to percentages set forth in the measure, which vary by county and recipient. Recipients include BART, Muni, Caltrain, AC Transit, Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority, San Francisco Bay Ferry, Golden Gate Transit, smaller bus operators in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, and county transportation agencies. Revenues would also support free and reduced-cost transit transfers, expansion of the Clipper START reduced-fare program, accessibility programs, mapping and wayfinding and transit priority projects and programs, and repavement projects for roads served by fixed-route transit. While the tax would be imposed throughout the District, the allocation of revenue generated in each county, and the authorized uses of those funds, would vary. For example, 64.70% of all revenues generated in Alameda County would be allocated to BART for transit operations expenses. By contrast, 84.37% of all revenues generated in Santa Clara County would be allocated to the Santa Clara Valley Transportation Authority for public transit expenses and roadway repavement projects on roads served by fixed-route transit. Such repavement projects would be an authorized use of measure revenues in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, but would not be authorized in the City and County of San Francisco. Revenue allocation is set forth in Section 12 of the measure. Tax revenues would be subject to accountability requirements in SB 63, which requires BART, Muni, AC Transit, and Caltrain to undergo financial efficiency reviews and adopt implementation plans and authorizes MTC to withhold funds from any of those operators for noncompliance. The measure would also require an independent oversight committee to review whether all revenues are distributed as required. The tax would become effective if approved by a majority of those voting on the measure throughout the entire District.
contests.yes_means: a vote to impose the tax described above for 14 years.
contests.no_means: a vote against imposing the tax.
contests.how_placed: On May 26, 2026, the “Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative” was submitted to election officials in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo, and Santa Clara counties, as well as the City and County of San Francisco. The petition included 306,288 unverified signatures. State law required 187,119 valid signatures to qualify the initiative for the ballot. This number is equal to 5% of the total number of registered voters within the District. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition showed that an estimated 235,503 signatures were valid. Because this number was greater than the 205,831 signature threshold, which represents 110% of the required number of signatures, the petition was found to be sufficient. On July 1, 2026, the District Elections Official certified that the petition contained enough valid signatures to qualify for the November 3, 2026 ballot.

sources.label: SF Voter Information Pamphlet, Nov 3 2026 (Dept. of Elections), p. 52

contests.title: Charter Amendment Measure
contests.subtitle: City of Oakland
contests.question: Shall the measure to amend Oakland's City Charter to, among other things, (1) make the Mayor the City's chief executive with a legislative veto, (2) empower the Council to override vetoes, confirm appointments of certain directors, and appoint an Independent Budget and Legislative Analyst, (3) affirm Councilmembers' right to acquire information from other City officials, (4) require Councilmembers to work full-time, and (5) empower the Public Ethics Commission to set salaries for all City elected officials using similar formulas, be adopted?
contests.summary:
Placed by the City Council; needs a simple majority. A "strong mayor" charter change:

• The Mayor, not the City Administrator, would run most departments and appoint most department heads. The Administrator keeps Human Resources and Finance and is still appointed by the Mayor with Council confirmation.
• The Council would confirm the heads of HR, Finance and infrastructure departments, could create an Independent Budget and Legislative Analyst office, could hold hearings and issue subpoenas, and councilmembers could relay constituent concerns to staff and get prompt answers. The misdemeanor for councilmember "interference" in administration is removed.
• The Mayor loses the tie-breaking vote but gains a veto over legislation and a line-item veto over the budget; six councilmembers can override.
• Councilmembers must work full time, with no conflicting outside jobs.
• The Public Ethics Commission would set Mayor and Council salaries, comparable to similar full-time officials in California.
• Ordinances could be published by newspaper or another Council-approved method within 15 days of passage.
contests.fiscal: The City Auditor estimates $2.0 million to $2.6 million in the first year: $288,000 to $867,000 more for Council salaries and benefits, and about $1.7 million to $1.8 million for the Independent Budget and Legislative Analyst office. No significant change is expected for the Mayor's pay.
contests.yes_means: Oakland moves to a strong-mayor charter with the changes above.
contests.no_means: Oakland keeps its current charter, with a City Administrator running departments.
contests.note: Rebuttal signers include Nate Miley, Nancy Nadel, Ralph Kanz, James Vann and Sharon Rose (rebutting YES), and Ernestine Nettles (League of Women Voters of Oakland), Kevin Jenkins, Michael Wallace, Libby Schaaf and Barbara Parker (rebutting NO).
contests.summary_label: What it does (our digest of the impartial analysis)

official_args.for: One accountable executive voters can judge, faster action on homelessness, public safety and illegal dumping, an independent budget analyst, a veto with a six-vote override, and full-time councilmembers. Supporters cite a public Charter Reform Working Group process with 1,150 residents' input.
official_args.against: Opponents call it a "strong mayor" power grab that Oakland tried from 1998 and dropped four years later: the executive needn't attend council meetings, future mayors could appoint allies, a veto plus losing the tie-break invites gridlock, and councilmembers get large raises. They note four councilmembers voted against placing it and favor a council-manager system instead.

contests.listed_supporters: Barbara Lee, Mayor of Oakland; Fred Blackwell, Former Oakland City Administrator; Isaac Abid, Board Chair, Revitalize East Bay; Richard Fuentes, Labor Leader/Small Business Owner; Sheryl Walton, Co-Chair, Block by Block Organizing Network
contests.listed_opponents: Ben Gould, Budget Advisory Commission Member and Organizer, Oakland Residents for Good Government; Pamela A. Drake, Community Advocate; Loren Taylor, Former Councilmember; Naomi Beryl Schiff, Community Advocate

contests.title: Real Property Tax Measure
contests.subtitle: City of Oakland
contests.question: Shall the measure amending Oakland's Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance to eliminate the foreclosure exception for all property transfers except transfers converting commercial property to certain housing or healthcare uses, transfers to community banking organizations, and certain transfers of residential properties of four units or less, and allowing the City Council to establish, amend, or remove foreclosure-related exceptions, raising approximately $4-$13 million annually pursuant to tax rates in Oakland Municipal Code section 4.20.020, beginning January 1, 2027 until repealed, be adopted?
contests.summary: Placed by the City Council; needs a simple majority; takes effect Jan 1, 2027. Oakland's transfer tax now exempts transfers through foreclosure or deed-in-lieu. The measure ends that general exemption, keeping exceptions only for (1) converting commercial property to certain housing or healthcare uses, (2) transfers to community banking organizations, and (3) homes of four units or fewer going to a person or family trust. The Council could later change those exceptions by ordinance. Taxable foreclosure transfers would be valued at fair market value and taxed at existing rates. The revenue is general-purpose.
contests.fiscal: The ballot question says about $4 million to $13 million a year. The City Auditor estimates $10.4 million to $13.8 million in the first year, based on commercial foreclosures in 2024 through mid-2026, with first-year costs of $592,900 to $651,100 (two tax auditors, partial supervisor, county collection fee).
contests.yes_means: Most foreclosure-related property transfers in Oakland pay the transfer tax.
contests.no_means: Foreclosure transfers stay exempt from Oakland's transfer tax.
contests.note: No argument against Measure FF was submitted.
contests.summary_label: What it does (our digest of the impartial analysis)

official_args.for: Families pay the transfer tax when they buy homes, but investors acquiring property through foreclosure don't; supporters say the loophole cost up to $25 million in the first half of 2026. Homeowners in foreclosure and ordinary homebuyers stay exempt, and buyers converting distressed buildings to housing or healthcare get relief.

contests.listed_supporters: Charlene Wang, District 2 Councilmember, Public Safety Chair; Barbara Lee, Mayor; Robert Apodaca, Co-Founder, Two Hundred for Homeownership and Casita Coalition; Raymond Lankford, Pastor, CEO, Oakland Private Industry Council
